'''Mövenpick Ice Cream''' ({{IPA|de|ˈmøːvənˌpɪk|lang}}) is a brand of [[ice cream]] of Swiss origin produced initially by [[Nestlé]]. Since 2016, [[Froneri]] - a joint venture between [[Nestlé]] and [[Froneri|R&R Ice Cream]] - manufactures it.

==History==
The first Mövenpick restaurant opened in [[Zürich]] on 19 July 1948 by [[Ueli Prager]]. By 1958, they had eight restaurants located throughout Switzerland.<ref name="mpick">{{cite web | url=http://www.moevenpick.com/moevenpick-gruppe/geschichte/?lang=en | title=Mövenpick History | access-date=20 January 2014 | archive-date=1 February 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201145039/http://www.moevenpick.com/moevenpick-gruppe/geschichte/?lang=en | url-status=dead }}</ref> Prager would remain operating manager of the Mövenpick group, now called [[Mövenpick Hotels & Resorts]], until 1991.

Originally, in the 1960s, the ice cream was produced by the Mövenpick group for restaurant sales only. The plant in [[Bursins]] was built in 1972, however, production has now been shifted to a larger unit in [[Rorschach, Switzerland|Rorschach]].{{citation needed|date=January 2014}}

In 1974, Mövenpick was licensed in Germany by ice cream manufacturer, [[Theo Schöller]], later known as Scholler Lebensmittel GmbH & Co KG. In 2002, EU regulators reviewed, and later approved, Nestlé's purchase of the Scholler Holding Group from Sudzucker, including licensing to sell Mövenpick in some European countries. The decision was made because while the merger would strengthen Nestlé's positioning in the ice cream market, [[Unilever]]'s role in the market would ensure continued strong competition in the sector.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=28 February 2002|title=Commission approves takeover of Scholler by Nestle. (European Union).(Scholler Holding Group purchased from Sudzucker AG)|journal=Dairy Markets|pages=3}}</ref>

In March 2000, Mövenpick acquired the [[Auckland]]-based Chateau Creme Delight Ice Cream company.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|title=Movenpick opens $8m Tamaki plant|last=McNabb|first=Denise|date=12 January 2001|work=[[The Dominion Post (Wellington)|The Dominion Post]]|page=15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Swiss icecream maker scoops up firm|last=Middlebrook|first=Libby|date=15 April 2000|work=New Zealand Herald}}</ref>

In 2002, Bauer was licensed to distribute and market Mövenpick in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=23 March 2002|title=Fife based American Pretzel Company used Expo as a launchpad|journal=The Grocer|pages=22}}</ref>

In April 2003, [[Nestlé]] bought the international rights for Mövenpick ice cream from the hotel group, and an independent business unit called "Swiss Premium Ice Cream" was created. The buy-out contract did not include the New Zealand manufacturing facilities.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=February 2003|title=Mövenpick sells ice its cream to Nestlé|journal=Dairy Industries International|volume= 68| issue =  2|pages=6}}</ref>

As of 2014, the business was operated by a subsidiary called "Nestlé Super Premium", headquartered in [[Vevey]], [[Switzerland]].<ref name="mpick2">{{cite web | url=http://www.moevenpick-icecream.com/gourmet/places/Pages/where.aspx | title=Mövenpick around the world | access-date=20 January 2014 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201225232/http://www.moevenpick-icecream.com/gourmet/places/Pages/where.aspx | archive-date=1 February 2014 }}</ref> In 2016, it was one of the brands that Nestlé contributed to a new joint venture with [[R&R Ice Cream]], called [[Froneri]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.livemint.com/Home-Page/XB5TR0nPM3sFN3Uxo1dQmM/Nestle-puts-sluggish-icecream-businesses-into-joint-venture.html|title=Nestle puts sluggish ice-cream businesses into joint venture|first=Corinne|last=Gretler|date=27 April 2016|website=mint|access-date=11 January 2020|archive-date=11 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200111132559/https://www.livemint.com/Home-Page/XB5TR0nPM3sFN3Uxo1dQmM/Nestle-puts-sluggish-icecream-businesses-into-joint-venture.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Production and distribution==
The main production site is in Switzerland. [[Halal#Foods|Halal]] production for the Middle East takes place at the Nestlé factory in Egypt.

The company has partnered licensing agreements in Germany, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1 April 2003|title=Nestle scores big merger coup in Europe, but gets FTC grief in United States market. (Ice Cream Scoops).(Federal Trade Commission is against the food conglomerate's acquisition of Dreyer's Grand Ice Cream)|journal=Quick Frozen Foods International|volume= 44| issue =  4|pages=83}}</ref>

In February 2006, Nestlé Schöller announced a newly patented type of [[Conche|"conching"]] process. The conchier process uses temperature reduction and slow, constant two-wave stirring to develop microscopic ice crystals and bubbles as the ice cream freezes. Minimising the need for large ice crystals reduces the required fat content by 30 to 40%, so the process creates low-fat ice cream, but with a creamy consistency and intense taste.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|date=1 January 2007|title=Spinning off its private-label operations, Nestle Scholler plans to focus on brands|journal=Quick Frozen Foods International}}</ref> The process was used to reduce the fat content in Bourbon Vanilla, Chocolate Chips, Erdbeer (strawberry) Cream and Maple Walnuts flavors. Machinery at the Uelzen factory was upgraded at a cost of 5 to 6 million euros.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Nestlé: New ice cream technology|date=28 February 2006|work=Lebensmittel Zeitung LZ/Net News}}</ref> In 2007, the conchier process was introduced to create "Decorative" category flavors with less than ten percent fat content: Cioccolata Straccietella, Caramel Brulee, Marzipan Chocolate and Chocolate Rum-Grape-Nut.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|date=1 April 2007|title=Gearing up for the new season, ice cream makers going exotic|journal=Quick Frozen Foods International}}</ref> This ice cream, in recent years, has shifted from sugar to glucose syrup in their ingredient list.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.moevenpick-icecream.com/swiss-chocolate#:~:text=Ingredients:+Whole+*milk*,,,+citrus+fibres,+salt,+natural|title=Swiss Chocolate|website=www.moevenpick-icecream.com|access-date=8 September 2020|archive-date=22 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200822033055/https://moevenpick-icecream.com/swiss-chocolate#:~:text=Ingredients:+Whole+*milk*,,,+citrus+fibres,+salt,+natural|url-status=live}}</ref>

In July 2017, Emerald Foods (Australia) Pty Ltd. purchased the master franchise rights for the Mövenpick parlours in Australia from [[Peters Ice Cream]]. Peters continued as the Mövenpick distributor for other channels in Australia.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.insideretail.com.au/blog/2017/07/04/emerald-foods-buys-movenpick-parlor-network/|title=Emerald Foods buys Mövenpick parlour network – Inside Retail|date=4 July 2017|work=Inside Retail|access-date=1 April 2018|language=en-US|archive-date=1 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180401213926/https://www.insideretail.com.au/blog/2017/07/04/emerald-foods-buys-movenpick-parlor-network/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Contracted production ===

==== Canada ====
In the 1990s, Mövenpick-branded products were made at plants in [[Simcoe, Ontario|Simcoe]], Ontario. Production was managed by Beatrice Foods, whose ice cream division was bought in 1994 by Good Humor-Popsicle (a child company of Unilever).<ref>{{Cite news|title=Getting the scoop on Breyer's|last=Marr|first=Lisa|date=4 July 1995|work=The Hamilton Spectator|page=C8}}</ref>

In 2001, Delicious Alternative Desserts Ltd. (DAD) received the contract to co-pack Mövenpick products in Canada, in packaging customised to the region.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Delicious Alternative Desserts Ltd. (DAD) and Movenpick Foods Canada Inc.|date=5 February 2001|work=The Food Institute Report|page=6}}</ref> DAD was placed in receivership in 2002.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Stoney Creek Dairy in receivership|last=Bell|first=Jocelyn|date=7 January 2002|work=Kitchener-Waterloo Record|page=C7}}</ref> Bankruptcy trustee KPMG continued limited production of Mövenpick at Stoney Creek Dairy, which was purchased by Better Beef Ltd. in February 2002. Better Beef was sold to Cargill Inc. in 2005, and the dairy was purchased by Creme Glacee Lambert in 2009, and closed in 2010.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thespec.com/news-story/2089898-high-costs-forced-stoney-creek-dairy-out/|title=High costs forced Stoney Creek Dairy out|date=20 May 2010|work=The Hamilton Spectator|access-date=31 March 2018|language=en-CA|archive-date=1 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180401003853/https://www.thespec.com/news-story/2089898-high-costs-forced-stoney-creek-dairy-out/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Egypt ====
In 2013, Nestlé upgraded their ice cream factory in Egypt, where Mövenpick ice creams are produced for export to Malaysia.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Nestlé invested CHF26 million extend its ice cream factory in Egypt|date=27 October 2013|work=Mist News}}</ref>

==== Germany ====
Nestlé produces Mövenpick ice cream in Germany, but sold part of its licensing and production facilities for trade brands to ice cream manufacturer Rosen Eiskrem GmbH of Waldfeucht-Haaren in January 2007.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Handelsblatt: Nestle to dispose of German ice-cream production (Nestle verkauft Eisproduktion in Deutschland)|date=22 September 2006|work=Handelsblatt|page=17}}</ref> The co-packing agreement and sale included plants in Nurnberg and Prenzlau. Nestlé Schöller remained at their Nurnberg headquarters, and retained their Uelzen plant.<ref name=":5" />

==== New Zealand ====
In September 1998, New Zealand-based Southern Fresh Milk Company received a $20 million 10-year contract from Mövenpick Asia-Pacific to produce and supply Mövenpick-branded ice cream to Asia and Australia. Southern Fresh was to create 11 ice cream flavors and 640,000 litres of ice cream annually. The contract did not include production or distribution of the desserts within New Zealand, as the importation and distribution contract was already allocated to [[Tip Top (ice cream)|Tip Top Foods]],<ref>{{Cite news|title=So Fresh wins $2m ice cream contract|last=Peart|first=Mark|date=24 September 1998|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref> which was intended to span 1988 to 2006.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Kiwi sells Swiss icecream to Asian market|last=McNabb|first=Denise|date=3 November 1999|work=[[The Dominion Post (Wellington)|The Dominion Post]]|page=24}}</ref> When the contract was awarded to Southern Fresh, Tip Top published an advertisement to clarify that they continued to hold the New Zealand market contract.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Tip Top cops Movenpick backlash|last=Simpson|first=Michele|date=12 November 1999|work=National Business Review}}</ref>

The Southern Fresh contract was later expanded to a revised $60 million,<ref>{{Cite news|title=City firm creams $60m deal|date=28 October 1999|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref> increasing to 16 flavors and 2.25 million litres of ice cream each year. The extra funds allowed for the expansion of a manufacturing plant with a dedicated Mövenpick production area.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Ice cream deal a triple scoop for south|last=Peart|first=Mark|date=29 October 1999|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref> Southern Fresh's contract allowed for sending the ice cream to Australia, Japan, and Singapore. Initial plans were to later export to South Korea, China, and Hong Kong.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Movenpick boss says South is tops for gourmet ice cream|last=Peart|first=Mark|date=6 January 2000|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref> One of the ice cream flavors produced for the Japanese market was Green Tea in 100ml containers.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Gourmet ice cream ready for Japan|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=22 September 2000|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=16}}</ref>

Southern Fresh purchased an additional factory in [[East Tamaki]], Auckland, in April 2000, which raised concerns that production work would be taken from the Invercargill factory.<ref name=":1" />

On 23 December 2000, 20 of the Southern Fresh workers at the Ettrick Street, [[Invercargill]], factory received notice that their employee contracts would not be renewed. The contractors were temporarily employed to produce Mövenpick ice cream.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Christmas sackings stun ice cream staff|last=Bellew|first=Vaneesa|date=23 December 2000|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Briefs|date=24 December 2000|work=[[Sunday Star-Times]]|page=A4}}</ref> One of the workers speculated in a ''[[The Southland Times|Southland Times]]'' article that the redundancies were linked to quality control. Southern Fresh executives countered that the job changes were a result of technical problems at the factory and market fluctuations.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Problems linked to job losses|last=Keen|first=Ryan|date=28 December 2000|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=3}}</ref> They later stated that the problem was more about "presentation",<ref>{{Cite news|title=Presentation problem led to loss of 20 factory jobs|last=Keen|first=Ryan|date=5 January 2000|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=3}}</ref> despite Mövenpick itself supplying the packaging to the factory.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|title=Movenpick buys plant up north|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=11 January 2001|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=2}}</ref>

The 2001 opening of the Auckland plant overrode the existing Tip Top Foods contract with Mövenpick.<ref name=":0" />

In April 2001, prior to Mövenpick's acquisition by Nestlé, executive Chris White moved from his Mövenpick Asia-Pacific chief executive role to a position at Nestlé.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|title=Scapegoat claim in ice cream row|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=4 April 2001|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=2}}</ref> White had previously assured staff at the Mövenpick Invercargill factory that the Southern Fresh contract would not be impacted by a new Auckland factory.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Southern Fresh hit by Movenpick contracts|date=7 April 2001|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref>

In April 2001, newspaper articles stated that Mövenpick ceased buying ice cream from Southern Fresh for the Japanese market, but the orders had ceased since November 2000. A Mövenpick executive stated that the companies were "...working through issues...". A Mövenpick executive stated that there were quality problems, but a Southern Fresh executive disputed this, noting the Japanese recession and that Southern Fresh were being used as a scapegoat for Mövenpick's marketing difficulties in Japan.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite news|title=20 ice cream staff laid off|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=7 April 2001|work=[[The Southland Times]]|page=1}}</ref> That same month, Southern Fresh dismissed 20 employees from the Invercargill factory as a result of the withdrawn Mövenpick orders.<ref name=":3" /> That same month, Southern Fresh stated in the media that they were owed millions of dollars<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|title=Dispute hots up as $60m ice cream contract ends|date=13 August 2001|work=Waikato Times|page=15}}</ref> by Mövenpick.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Southern Fresh considers sellout|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=20 April 2001|work=The Southland Times|page=1}}</ref> There were arbitration meetings between Mövenpick and Southern Fresh in August 2001, which acknowledged that their contract lapsed in November 2000.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite news|title=Movenpick dispute remains unresolved|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=13 August 2001|work=The Southland Times|page=4}}</ref> In September 2001, Mövenpick stated that all issues between the parties had been resolved.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Cash boost saves So Fresh sellout|last=Sutton|first=Michelle|date=15 September 2001|work=The Southland Times|page=3}}</ref> In February 2002, Southern Fresh chief executive Alasdair McLachlan described the Mövenpick deal as "disastrous",<ref>{{Cite news|title=Decision due on Southern Fresh|last=Potter|first=Karen|date=19 February 2002|work=The Southern Times|page=4}}</ref> identifying it as "Mövenpick's [contract] failure is what killed us.", in being the main contributing factor for Southern Fresh's significant loan, and later buyout, by dairy company [[Mainland (cheese)|Mainland]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Milk chief has regrets over buyout|last=Bellew|first=Vaneesa|date=20 March 2002|page=1}}</ref> Mainland closed the Invercargill factory in July 2002.<ref>{{Cite news|title=City milk factory to close|last=Bellew|first=Vaneesa|date=20 June 2002|work=The Southland Times|page=2}}</ref>

At the time of the 2003 acquisition of Mövenpick by Nestlé, Chateau Creme Delight Ice Cream company continued to produce Mövenpick ice creams under license. The New Zealand rights were not included in the Nestlé contract, and Nestlé did not have their own production facilities in the country.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Nestle acquires Movenpick rights – except in NZ|date=27 January 2003|work=Foodweek}}</ref> Mövenpick retained the Chateau rights because it wanted to increase its presence in the Asia Pacific region.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Little guys hold onto their milkpails|date=24 March 2003|work=New Zealand Herald}}</ref> In October 2003, International Dairy Ventures (IDV) purchased the New Zealand operations of Chateau, including the Nestlé-licensed Mövenpick productions and the Mövenpick store in Mission Bay, Auckland.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Milk movers target top ice cream market|last=Stringleman|first=Hugh|date=17 October 2003|work=National Business Review}}</ref>

Mövenpick products were later made by Emerald Foods, a company owned by Mövenpick until December 2003, when it was sold to the Emerald Group.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Emerald takes full control of NZ Natural|date=25 July 2005|work=Inside Retailing}}</ref> In December 2005, Emerald Group CEO [[Diane Foreman]] noted a supply challenge, in that Emerald was contractually obliged to buy all raw materials from Swiss-based Mövenpick, to make licensed Mövenpick products.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Finger-lickin' good|last=Owen|first=Wilson|date=14 December 2005|work=The Independent Business Weekly}}</ref> In late 2009, Emerald signed a contract with Mövenpick for a further four years.<ref>{{Cite news|title=A woman of substance|last=Scherer|first=Karyn|date=16 October 2009|work=New Zealand Herald}}</ref>

The ice cream making subsidiary of the Emerald Group was then sold to Emerald Foods Group (HK) in April 2015.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Food firm sold|date=11 June 2015|work=The Nelson Mail|page=6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Getting the best out of all those zeros: Diane Foreman|last=Ryan|first=Holly|date=22 August 2015|work=The New Zealand Herald|page=C003}}</ref> [[File:Mövenpick Ice Cream Boutique.jpg|thumbnail|Mövenpick "Boutique" in Taiwan]]

==== Pakistan ====
In the 1990s, Ambrosia International Limited (Pvt) (AIL) began a licensing agreement with Mövenpick to produce their branded ice creams in Pakistan.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1 January 1998|title=Ice cream industry in Pakistan (Industry Overview)|journal=Economic Review|volume= 29| issue =  1|pages=37}}</ref> The JOFA Group has been the exclusive franchiser for the brand since 2002.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|date=31 May 2012|title=Cool treats|journal=Slogan|volume= 17}}</ref>

==== Saudi Arabia ====
From the late 1980s until 2009, [[SADAFCO]] produced Mövenpick-branded products at plants in Jeddah, Riyadh, Dammam, and Madinah. However, starting in 2011, Mohammed Khaled Alkhulaidi Trading Establishment ("MKKTE") became the exclusive franchiser of the brand in Saudi Arabia, importing Mövenpick ice cream products and distributing them to hotels and through different points of sale across the kingdom.<ref>{{Cite news|title=SADAFCO Movenpick partnership from strength to strength|date=28 January 2002|work=Middle East Company News}}</ref>

==== Sweden ====
In 2011, Swedish ice cream manufacturer Triumf Glass introduced Mövenpick Classic flavors to the Swedish market in 900ml packaging. Flavors included Almond & Vanilla, Caramelita, Maple Walnut, Strawberry, Swiss Chocolate, and Vanilla Dream.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Sweden: Triumf Glass introduces new ice creams from Mövenpick|date=18 May 2011|work=Esmerk Swedish News|page=41}}</ref>

==== United States ====
Mövenpick-branded ice cream was first produced in America in the late 1980s by Sunnyside Farms Dairy at a plant in [[Turlock, California|Turlock]], California.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Honer|first=Clem|date=1 May 1989|title=Automation worth arguing for; mid-valley dairy's new ice cream plant promises to move the industry forward|journal=Dairy Foods|pages=51}}</ref>

=== Yogurts ===
Premium low-fat yogurts are created under the Mövenpick brand, they were first sold through Germany's Bauer brand in 2013.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=December 2013|title=Pure passion from Mövenpick|journal=Dairy Industries International|volume= 78| issue =  12|pages=12}}</ref> In 2017, the yogurt limited edition Winter flavors included cherry-chocolate, vanilla, café nougatine and plum-cinnamon.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=November 2017|title=Winter season yogurts|journal=Dairy Industries International|volume= 82| issue =  11|pages=12}}</ref>

==Availability==
While Mövenpick ice cream was originally only produced for their branded restaurants in Switzerland, as at 2011, it was sold in almost 40 countries.<ref name=":8" /> Products are sold through retail channels, parlours and hotels or restaurants.

The branded franchised stores ("dessert cafes", parlours, "Mövenpick boutiques", or "ice cream galleries") are in many different countries. The stores have also been named "Ice Dreams", for their focus on incorporating Mövenpick ice creams into dessert recipes.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Ice cream trade sure to delight|date=7 September 2009|work=The Courier-Mail|page=38}}</ref> In 2010, the national retail manager for the brand in Australia, Dennis Koorey, described Mövenpick's parlours as a "...dine-in dessertery."<ref name=":7">{{Cite news|title=Movenpick moves on with rebrand|last=Bridge|first=Carla|date=12 March 2010|work=Inside Retailing}}</ref>

=== Retail ===
In 1989, Mövenpick attempted to introduce their ice creams in Canada, but encountered local production difficulties due to dairy industry buy-outs. In July 1992, they again began selling their products in Canadian supermarkets, but with revised packaging. Instead of 1-litre rectangular brick-size packages, the ice cream was packaged in [[Häagen-Dazs]]-style 500ml tubs.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Movenpick ups scoop stakes|last=Papoe|first=Bob|date=22 July 1992|work=The Toronto Star|page=F3}}</ref>

In 1999, six flavors of Mövenpick ice creams were introduced to the Japanese market at convenience stores, through a Japanese subsidiary company.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=14 October 1999|title=Movenpick enters ice cream market|journal=Dairy Markets Weekly|pages=11}}</ref>

In 2008, four flavors (Swiss Chocolate, Maple Walnut, Panna Cotta, White Peach & Redcurrant) of Mövenpick ice creams in 500ml containers, began being sold in England's Tesco supermarkets.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Mövenpick luxury ice cream hits UK|date=8 March 2008|work=The Grocer|pages=56–57}}</ref> In 2013, Mövenpick made an agreement with England's Ocado supermarkets to sell four flavors (Caramelita, Swiss Chocolate, Vanilla Dream and Strawberry) in 900ml containers.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Mövenpick ice cream tubs go on sale at Ocado|last=Mileham|first=Arabella|date=7 September 2013|work=The Grocer}}</ref>

In 2007, [[Hjem-IS|Hemglass]] began a contract as the exclusive seller of Mövenpick products in Sweden, at their ice cream vans.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Sweden: Hemglass to sell Mövenpick's products|date=16 April 2007|work=Esmerk Swedish News|page=16}}</ref>

In 2016, Mövenpick again began selling ice cream in 500ml tubs in supermarkets. Ice cream flavors offered included Vanilla Dream, Swiss Chocolate, Strawberry, Caramelita, Maple Walnut and Tiramisu. Sorbet flavors included Raspberry & Strawberry and Passionfruit & Mango.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Riley|first=Lisa|date=14 May 2016|title=Mövenpick launches 500ml sharing tub format into Ocado|journal=The Grocer|pages=46}}</ref>

== Media coverage ==
In June 1996, in response to complaints by English MPs and parliamentary staff, Mövenpick ice creams were removed from the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] menu. The branded ice creams had been available on the menu for two days prior to removal. The complainants alleged that it was unpatriotic for the German-produced Swiss brand to be sold in the parliament in the midst of [[bovine spongiform encephalopathy]]-related export bans on English beef in Germany.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Hans off our ices!|date=30 June 1996|work=People|page=11}}</ref>

In October 2006, a customer complaint letter was published in the [[The New Zealand Herald|New Zealand Herald]]. The complainant alleged that staff at the Auckland Mövenpick store refused to serve a pregnant customer a free glass of tap water, as the company policy was to sell mineral water.<ref>{{Cite news|title=That ain't no way to treat a lady growing a baby: A reader was happy to spend...|date=3 October 2006|work=New Zealand Herald}}</ref> Two days later, the same newspaper noted that the company policy had been changed to allow the serving of free tap water.<ref>{{Cite news|title=A story on Slate.com tells how companies manage to 'save very little money...' |date=5 October 2006|work=New Zealand Herald}}</ref>

In September 2010, in an article in [[The Times]], Mövenpick's tagline of "The art of Swiss ice cream" was used as an example in the proposed "Swissness Bill". The Swiss Government proposed to legally determine the requirements for products to be advertised as "made in Switzerland".<ref>{{Cite news|title=Knives are out for those who abuse what it means to be Swiss; Legal test for 'Made in Switzerland'|last=Sage|first=Adam|date=4 September 2010|work=The Times|page=51}}</ref>

In June 2012, the Finnish Consumer Agency analysed the fruit, sugar and fat content of chocolate and strawberry ice creams sold from kiosks. Mövenpick's Swiss Chocolate flavor was found to have the highest amount of fat, among the brands and flavors tested.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Finland: Content of kiosk ice creams varies greatly|date=7 June 2012|work=Esmerk Finnish News|pages=12–13}}</ref>

In August 2016, Russia's consumer protection organisation Roscontrol found that Mövenpick ice creams contained more sucrose than indicated on the packaging.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Russia: Roscontrol examines quality of plombir|date=10 August 2016|work=Esmerk Russian News}}</ref>

In August 2017, Mövenpick raised prices of their ice creams in Switzerland by 2.5 per cent, to absorb increased costs of vanilla beans. The price increased after [[Cyclone Enawo]] devastated vanilla crops in [[Madagascar]], as well as the increasing popularity of the ingredient.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Vanilla price surge hits high-end ice cream consumers|last=Terazono|first=Emiko|date=22 August 2017|work=Financial Times}}</ref>

extract: Mövenpick Ice Cream (German: [ˈmøːvənˌpɪk]) is a brand of ice cream of Swiss origin produced initially by Nestlé. Since 2016, Froneri - a joint venture between Nestlé and R&R Ice Cream - manufactures it.
